title: rack-aware-comm-windowing-notes
content:
Summary:

This doc captures our exploratory run investigating rack-aware communication windowing (RA-CW) and an "ejector" idea for shaping inter-rack traffic during multi-GPU LLM inference. The goal was to see whether small, time-boxed windows for cross-rack NCCL collectives, combined with aggressive intra-rack prioritization, reduce tail latency for small-batch, high-concurrency streaming workloads without losing steady-state throughput.

Motivation / hypothesis:
- We repeatedly see long tails when a few requests trigger cross-rack NVLink->NVSwitch->PCIe paths while the cluster is saturated.
- Hypothesis A: If we gate cross-rack collective start times into short windows (e.g., 2-5ms), each window will serialize some cross-rack transfers and reduce microburst contention on spine links.
- Hypothesis B: Allowing intra-rack traffic to proceed with tighter pacing (higher priority) during those windows preserves most short-request latency while deferring larger cross-rack KV-cache fills to a controlled boundary.
- Ejector idea: if a cross-rack collective would exceed a runtime-configured bytes threshold, eject the request to a compatible local model replicate (fallback) to keep latency SLOs.

Testbed:
- Cluster: 8 nodes, 4 nodes per rack (rack A, rack B), each node: 8xA100-80GB (PCIe+NVSwitch fabric inside node), dual 200Gb/s NICs for inter-rack.
- OS/stack: Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.2, NCCL 2.18, custom runtime branch (ra-cw-experiments).
- Model: truncated 7B decoder-only (approx 12GB sharded), per-shard tensor-parallel (TP=2), pipeline-parallel 1 (no pipeline stages for this probe), kv-cache across tensors via sharded KV layout.
- Workload: streaming chat requests, token-gen target ~40 tokens, arrival pattern: Poisson with mean QPS=120, and a synthetic burst case where 40 concurrent requests arrive in 200ms.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency for response-ready (first token), average tokens/sec throughput, interconnect utilization from switch counters, NCCL timeline traces, and CPU host PCIe stall counters.

Configs tried:
1) baseline: no windowing, existing backpressure and NCCL settings (control).
2) fixed-window 5ms: cross-rack collectives only start at discrete 5ms boundaries (aligned at runtime tick).
3) fixed-window 2ms: as above with 2ms windows.
4) adaptive-window: measured cross-rack request rate -> window size scales (min 1ms, max 8ms) to maintain target cross-rack concurrency <= 2.
5) ejector-enabled: when collective estimated transfer > 1.2GB, attempt eject to local replica else proceed with adaptive-window.

Key observations (raw):
- Baseline: burst case p99-first-token = 1.83s, average throughput 86 tokens/s, switch spine link saturated at 92% for 80ms during burst, NCCL fatal retries observed 2x per burst (retries correlated with host PCIe queue full events).
- 5ms window: p99-first-token dropped to 820ms, throughput 79 tokens/s (steady-state drop ~8%), spine link peaks reduced to 66%, NCCL retries reduced to zero in observed bursts.
- 2ms window: p99-first-token ~940ms (worse than 5ms), throughput 82 tokens/s, more frequent small stalls on host observed (higher scheduling overhead).
- adaptive-window: p99-first-token ~720ms, throughput 80 tokens/s, link peaks ~60-70% and smoother.
- ejector-enabled (with adaptive-window): p99-first-token 420ms for requests that ejected to local replica; overall p99-first-token across all requests 590ms, throughput drop ~12% but tail QoS much improved.

Interpretation:
- Windowing reduces tail caused by cross-rack microbursts: serialization reduces contention on spine links and avoids concurrent large DMA bursts that saturate PCIe hosts.
- Too small a window (2ms) increases scheduling/latency jitter because we introduce additional synchronization points at a timescale comparable to GPU kernel launch/queue affinities — overhead outweighs serialization benefit.
- Adaptive windowing that targets a small cross-rack concurrency (<=2) produced best tradeoff in our tests.
- Ejector approach provides the strongest tail improvement for user-visible latency at the cost of slightly lower overall tokens/sec and increased model divergence risk (replica mismatch). This is promising for SLO-first tiers.

Profiling notes / evidence snippets:
- NCCL trace snippet (baseline burst): repeated "AllGather start" timestamps clustered within 1-2ms windows from 30+ ranks -> corresponds to NIC TX queue growth.
- Switch counters: spine port 3 counters show step function increase aligned with burst arrival (80ms window).
- Host PCIe: device queue full events recorded at +30ms into burst, matching NCCL retry logs.
- Kernel scheduling overlap: when windows enforced, we see sustained compute overlap in intra-rack ranks while cross-rack ranks are blocked on barrier, improving GPU occupancy profile for short requests.

Open questions and concerns:
- Ejector semantics: how to pick compatible fallback replica? Option list: same model lower precision quantized replica, pinned local serving replica, or CPU fallback. Each has quality/cost tradeoffs.
- Safety for stateful KV-cache: ejecting requests that expect warmed KV-cache might change outputs. Need cache-warm policies or deterministic fallback conditions.
- Interaction with NCCL P2P algorithms: windowing effectively serializes launches; might subvert NCCL auto-tuning — need to test with newer NCCL versions and nvlink topologies.
- Scheduler finger-grain: we add a scheduler tick at 1ms resolution; what is the CPU overhead at cluster scale (100s nodes)?

Actionable next steps:
- Short-term (1 sprint): implement adaptive-windowing with config knobs exposed in runtime. Add telemetry: cross-rack concurrency gauge, per-window bytes, and percent-ejected.
- Mid-term: prototype ejector fallback policies (local quantized replica + soft-consistency flag). Do an A/B on a small customer tenant.
- Measurement: run a 48-node run (3 racks) to validate whether benefits scale; add NCCL 2.18 -> 2.21 comparison matrix.
- Risk analysis: add rollout guard rails (start in canary, SLO alerting, auto-disable if throughput drop > 20% for 10m).

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- Add Git patch to runtime to expose per-collective estimated transfer bytes (used by ejector).
- Add unit test for window alignment across nodes (clock sync tolerance test).
- File long-run logs in GCS bucket: gs://redwood-ci/ra-cw/2025-01-20/ (raw traces, NCCL logs, switch counters).

Appendix (short table):

Config      | p50-first | p95-first | p99-first | throughput (tokens/s) | spine-peak
baseline    | 86ms      | 320ms     | 1830ms    | 86                   | 92%
5ms-window  | 92ms      | 210ms     | 820ms     | 79                   | 66%
2ms-window  | 98ms      | 275ms     | 940ms     | 82                   | 70%
adaptive    | 88ms      | 190ms     | 720ms     | 80                   | 65%
adaptive+ejector | 75ms | 120ms     | 590ms     | 76                   | 60%

(Interpret table as approximate — see raw logs for full distributions.)

Conclusion:
- Rack-aware windowing is a viable operational knob to reduce tail latency for multi-rack LLM inference under bursty request patterns. Adaptive sizing is important to avoid overhead; ejector fallbacks further reduce user-facing tails for SLO-sensitive tiers.
- Next engineering work should focus on safe ejector semantics, telemetry, and a canary rollout plan.

If useful I can convert this into a short slide deck for Eng Review early next week.

End of note.
